chapter: Second interview: bass, Parker and Miles
title: The decline of real jam sessions
summary: Jam sessions began as release for big-band players; booking agents and Norman Granz turned them into shows.

story.theme_name: Coming to New York: clubs, jams, and making it
story.community_name: Making it in New York: arrival, clubs and the scene

blocks.x: Yeah. You say, you didn't enjoy playing a whole lot.
I did when I was younger.
That's when the guys used to have battles, go out to somebody. There's no more jam sessions.
There haven't been jam sessions for, I guess, at least -- what, 20, 30 years?
Why did the jam sessions kind of disappear?
Well, see, the agents for booking ham sessions (inaudible). They were trying to accomplish what was going on in jam sessions. Before that, there was guys
working in the big bands, travelling around. And they would get together because (inaudible) find someplace to play, to get a release from the tensions of reading music.
And then as they began to really book them as jam sessions, they weren't jam sessions anymore.
It's like Norman Granz, he jazz at the Philharmonic as if it were jazz.
